title: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES
alt_titles: CATARACT 2, MULTIPLE TYPES, WITH OR WITHOUT MICROCORNEA

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that cataract-2 of multiple types (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the gene encoding gamma-C-crystallin (CRYGC) on chromosome 2q33-q35.

checks.claim: Cataract-2 of multiple types (CTRCT2), with or without microcornea, is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CRYGC gene encoding gamma-C-crystallin.
checks.evidence_quote: To our knowledge, these findings are the first evidence of an involvement of CRYGC and support the role of CRYGD in human cataract formation.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports CRYGC involvement in human cataract. It does not mention heterozygosity, multiple cataract types or microcornea; the full text was not supplied.

checks.claim: The CRYGC gene is located on chromosome 2q33-q35.
checks.evidence_quote: We have localized the cataracts to a 19-cM interval on chromosome 2q33-q35 including the gamma-crystallin gene cluster.
checks.explanation: The gamma-crystallin cluster, which includes CRYGC, lies in 2q33-q35.

paragraphs.text: CTRCT2 is an autosomal dominant congenital cataract caused by mutation in the CRYGC gene. The cataracts reported in families with CRYGC mutations have been of several morphologic types, including Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus, variable zonular pulverulent cataract, lamellar cataract, and nuclear cataract (Lubsen et al., 1987; Ren et al., 2000; Gonzalez-Huerta et al., 2007). In some families the nuclear cataracts have been accompanied by microcornea (Zhang et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2012).

checks.evidence_quote: A family with autosomal dominant primary congenital cataract associated with a CRYGC mutation: evidence of clinical heterogeneity.
checks.explanation: The title states an autosomal dominant congenital cataract associated with a CRYGC mutation.

checks.explanation: The paper describes a Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus but shows only linkage to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster. It does not identify a CRYGC mutation.

checks.evidence_quote: A 5-base insertion in the gammaC-crystallin gene is associated with autosomal dominant variable zonular pulverulent cataract.

checks.evidence_quote: This mutation has been associated with the phenotype of lamellar cataract but is also considered a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the NCBI database.
checks.explanation: The paper notes lamellar cataract in an earlier family with the CRYGC mutation.

checks.claim: Cataracts in families with CRYGC mutations include nuclear cataract.
checks.evidence_quote: we described a family with nuclear congenital cataract that segregated the CRYGC missense mutation c.502C>T.

paragraphs.text: Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family with 48 of 138 individuals known to be affected with autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. Of 53 family members examined, 28 had congenital cataracts: in 19 the cataract was unilateral (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and in 9 it was bilateral. The clinically unaffected eye of patients with unilateral cataract showed no lenticular opacity on detailed slit-lamp examination. Severity ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 visual acuity and bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 visual acuity in both eyes to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts requiring early surgical removal. Including historical data on unexamined members, there were 48 affected members (28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 unexamined obligate carriers). Scott et al. (1994) noted that hereditary cataracts are typically symmetric, and that this family showed apparently random expression of the gene as unilateral or bilateral cataract.

paragraphs.text: Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation Chinese family, residing in a relatively isolated region of northern China, with 6 members affected by nuclear cataracts and microcornea in the absence of other ocular or systemic abnormalities. Affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts consisting of a central nuclear opacity affecting the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nucleus of the lens, with congenitally small eyeballs and corneas approximately 9 to 10 mm in diameter. Every affected individual had visual acuity of hand movement in front of the eye, as well as nystagmus and amblyopia.

paragraphs.text: Guo et al. (2012) reported a 4-generation Chinese family in which 6 members had isolated bilateral nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The nuclear opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and corneal diameter was approximately 9 mm in all affected individuals. The proband was diagnosed with bilateral nuclear cataract and microcornea at age 8 years, when he underwent iridectomy on both eyes; his left eye underwent phacoemulsification and intraocular lens implantation at age 38, and his best corrected visual acuity was 0.08 in the right eye and FC/30cm in the left. Other affected members were diagnosed at 6 months, 1 year, and 13 years of age, and 1 had cataract extraction at 6 years of age. Intraocular pressure was normal, nystagmus and amblyopia were observed in all patients, and there was no history of related systemic abnormalities.

paragraphs.text: In the family with Coppock-like cataract, Brakenhoff et al. (1994) mapped the linked polymorphic TaqI sites to a 15-kb region encompassing the gamma-D (CRYGD) gene and the gamma-E pseudogene (CRYGE). The gamma-D gene cloned from the cataract chromosome was functionally equivalent to the wildtype allele, whereas the pseudogene contained a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box that caused a 10-fold increase in promoter activity, raising its expression to 30% of that of the gamma-D gene. Brakenhoff et al. (1994) proposed that reactivation of the pseudogene, with overexpression of a predicted 6-kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment, could be the cause of the cataract.

paragraphs.text: Heon et al. Heon et al. (1999) noted that there was no direct evidence that upregulation of a pseudogene causes cataract.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a family with primary nuclear congenital cataract, Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) identified a heterozygous c.502C-T transition in the CRYGC gene, resulting in an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The healthy family members and 170 unrelated controls had normal sequence of the CRYGA-D gene cluster. The authors noted that this mutation had previously been associated with lamellar cataract but was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database, and concluded that R168W is disease-causing.

agent.process_note: I opened all 10 files. Two had full text (Zhang et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2012) and I read both in full. Seven had abstracts only, and Santhiya et al. (2002) had only a title, so I did not cite it. The Heon et al. (1999) abstract does not name the CRYGC missense change in the Coppock-like family. The T5P/c.13A>C designation therefore comes only from the reviews in Zhang et al. (2009) and Guo et al. (2012). The c.123-128insGCGGC notation for the 5-bp duplication comes from Guo's table, not from Ren et al. (2000). The C109X (c.327C>A) mutation appears only in those reviews, with no primary patient data, so I did not give it an allelic-variant entry. I did not state that Ren's family is the same as Scott's, because Ren's abstract says only that the family was 'previously described'. No ancestry is given for the Lubsen or Gonzalez-Huerta families. No gene MIM number was supplied, so the intro has no MIM number, and the chromosome location (2q33-q35) is taken from the papers.
